en: Majjhima Nikāya 144,
Channovādasutta.
Thus have I heard:
At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels’ Feeding Place.
Now on that occasion the Venerable Sāriputta, the Venerable Mahācunda, and the Venerable Channa were dwelling on Mount Gijjhakūṭa.
On that occasion the Venerable Channa was afflicted, suffering, and gravely ill.
Then, in the evening, the Venerable Sāriputta emerged from seclusion and approached the Venerable Mahācunda. Having approached, he said this to the Venerable Mahācunda:
"Come, friend Cunda, let us go to the Venerable Channa to inquire after his health.
"Very well, friend," the Venerable Mahācunda replied to the Venerable Sāriputta.
Then the Venerable Sāriputta and the Venerable Mahācunda approached the Venerable Channa. Having approached, they exchanged greetings with the Venerable Channa.
When they had concluded their polite and courteous conversation, they sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, the Venerable Sāriputta said this to the Venerable Channa:
“Friend Channa, I hope you are bearing up, I hope you are getting by? I hope your painful feelings are subsiding and not increasing, and that their subsiding is apparent, not their increase?
“Friend Sāriputta, I am not bearing up, I am not getting by. My painful feelings are severe; they are increasing and not subsiding, and their increase is apparent, not their subsiding.”
"Friend Sāriputta, it is just as if a strong man were to strike one on the head with a sharp spear; even so, friend Sāriputta, violent winds are piercing my head.
It is not endurable for me, friend Sāriputta, nor can I maintain myself. My severe painful feelings are increasing, not subsiding; their increase is apparent, not their subsiding."
"Friend Sāriputta, it is just as if a strong man were to wrap a tight leather thong around one’s head and twist it; even so, friend Sāriputta, I have an intense, piercing pain in my head.
It is not bearable for me, friend Sāriputta, nor can I endure it. My sharp painful feelings are increasing, not subsiding; their increase is apparent, not their subsiding.
It is just as if, friend Sāriputta, a skilled butcher or a butcher’s apprentice were to use a sharp carving knife..."
“...as if they were cutting my belly with a saw; even so, friend Sāriputta, violent winds cut through my belly.
It is neither bearable nor sustainable for me, friend Sāriputta. My intense painful feelings are increasing, not subsiding; their increase is apparent, not their subsiding.
It is as if, friend Sāriputta, two strong men were seizing a weaker man by his various limbs...”
"Having taken them, they would heat them in a pit of glowing embers and burn them all over. Even so, friend Sāriputta, there is an excessive burning in my body.
It is neither bearable nor sustainable for me, friend Sāriputta. My sharp painful feelings are increasing, not subsiding; their increase is apparent, not their subsiding."
“Friend Sāriputta, I shall take up the blade; I have no desire for life.
“Venerable Channa, do not take up the blade.
Let the Venerable Channa live on. We wish for the Venerable Channa to live on.”
If the Venerable Channa lacks suitable food, I will seek out suitable food for the Venerable Channa.
If the Venerable Channa lacks suitable medicine, I will seek out suitable medicine for the Venerable Channa.
If the Venerable Channa lacks a suitable attendant, I will attend upon the Venerable Channa.
“Venerable Channa has drawn the sword.
Let the venerable Channa live on! We wish for the venerable Channa to live.
“Friends, it is not that I lack suitable food;”
It is not that I lack suitable medicines,
nor that I lack appropriate attendants; rather,
friend Sāriputta, for a long time I have served the Teacher with what is pleasing, never with what is displeasing.
"For this is appropriate for a disciple, friend Sāriputta: that he should attend upon the Teacher with what is pleasing, not with what is displeasing.
'The bhikkhu Channa will take up the knife blamelessly'—thus, friend Sāriputta, you should remember it.
"We would ask the venerable Channa about a certain point, if the venerable Channa would grant us the opportunity to answer his question."
“Ask, friend Sāriputta; having heard, I shall know.
“Friend Channa, do you regard the eye, eye-consciousness, and the things cognizable by eye-consciousness as ‘This is mine, this am I, this is my self’?
Do you regard the ear, friend Channa, ear-consciousness, and so forth...”
The nose, friend Channa, and nose-consciousness...
the tongue, friend Channa, and tongue-consciousness...
the body, friend Channa, and body-consciousness...
“Friend Channa, do you regard the mind, mind-consciousness, and the phenomena cognizable by mind-consciousness as ‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self’?
“Friend Sāriputta, I regard the eye, eye-consciousness, and the phenomena cognizable by eye-consciousness as ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.
Friend Sāriputta, [I regard] the ear... [and so on].”
The nose, friend Sāriputta… the tongue,
friend Sāriputta… the body, friend Sāriputta…
“Friend Sāriputta, regarding the mind, mind-consciousness, and the phenomena cognizable by mind-consciousness, I regard them thus: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.

“Friend Channa, having seen what, and having directly known what, regarding the eye, eye-consciousness, and the phenomena cognizable by eye-consciousness, do you regard the eye, eye-consciousness, and the phenomena cognizable by eye-consciousness thus: ‘This is not mine...’?”
"Do you regard it thus: 'This is not I, this is not my self'?
"In the ear, friend Channa, in ear-consciousness...
in the nose, friend Channa, in nose-consciousness..."
Friend Channa, having seen what in the tongue,
in tongue-consciousness… in the body, friend Channa, in body-consciousness… in the mind,
friend Channa, in mind-consciousness, and in the phenomena cognizable by mind-consciousness, [did you see this]? What [did you see]?
“Having directly known the mind, mind-consciousness, and the phenomena cognizable by mind-consciousness, do you regard them thus:
‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self’?
“In the eye, friend Sāriputta, in eye-consciousness, and in the phenomena cognizable by eye-consciousness, [I see] cessation.”
Having seen cessation and having directly known it, I regard the eye, eye-consciousness, and the phenomena cognizable by eye-consciousness thus:
‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.
[In the same way,] friend Sāriputta, regarding the ear, ear-consciousness...
In the nose, friend Sāriputta, in nose-consciousness...
in the tongue, friend Sāriputta, in tongue-consciousness...
in the body, friend Sāriputta, in body-consciousness...

“Friend Sāriputta, having seen cessation in the mind, in mind-consciousness, and in the phenomena cognizable by mind-consciousness, and having directly known that cessation, I regard the mind, mind-consciousness, and the phenomena cognizable by mind-consciousness as:
‘This is not mine; this I am not; this is not my self.’”
When this was said, the Venerable Mahācunda said this to the Venerable Channa:
“Therefore, friend Channa, this too is the teaching of the Blessed One that should be kept in mind for all time:
‘For one who is dependent there is wavering; for one who is independent there is no wavering.’”
When equanimity exists, there is tranquility;
when tranquility exists, there is no inclination.
When there is no inclination, there is no coming and going.
"When there is no coming and going, there is no passing away and being reborn.
When there is no passing away and being reborn, there is neither this world nor the world beyond, nor anything in between these two.
This, indeed, is the end of suffering."
Then the Venerable Sāriputta and the Venerable Mahācunda, having exhorted the Venerable Channa with this instruction, rose from their seats and departed.
Not long after the Venerable Sāriputta and the Venerable Mahācunda had left, the Venerable Channa drew a weapon against himself.

Then the Venerable Sāriputta approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the Venerable Sāriputta said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, the Venerable Channa has taken up a blade.
What is his destination, what is his future state?
“Sāriputta, did not the bhikkhu Channa declare right here before you that he was free from blame?”
“Venerable sir, there is a Vajjian village named Pubbajirā.
There, the venerable Channa has families who are his friends, families who are his intimates, and families who are his associates.
“These indeed, Sāriputta, are the families who are friends, intimates, and associates of the bhikkhu Channa.”
“Sāriputta, I do not say that one is ‘blameworthy’ on account of this much alone.
Rather, Sāriputta, when someone casts off this body and takes up another body, I say that person is ‘blameworthy.
That does not apply to the bhikkhu Channa.”
“‘The bhikkhu Channa, being blameless, took up the knife’—thus, Sāriputta, you should remember this.
This is what the Blessed One said.
The venerable Sāriputta, being uplifted, rejoiced in the words of the Blessed One.
The Discourse of Advice to Channa is finished; it is the second.
